content: The study was conducted in both urban and rural areas across five provinces in South Africa, a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis (TB), TB/HIV co-infection, and multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). Children were eligible for enrollment if they met all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria. Eligibility criteria for children included: Being under 5 years of age (as per protocol). Residing primarily in the household of an adult MDR-TB index patient or having significant exposure to such a contact. Parental or legal guardian consent for HIV testing and study enrollment. Assent from children or adolescents aged 7 years or older. For children aged 5–17 years, a positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) test (Quantiferon-Gold Plus, Qiagen) was required unless the child was HIV-positive. Children under 5 years of age were eligible regardless of IGRA status. All HIV-positive children under 18 years of age were eligible regardless of IGRA status. Exclusion criteria for children included: Current TB disease. Known pregnancy. Inability to take oral medication. Body weight below 3 kg. Unwillingness or inability to participate in follow-up. Current breastfeeding. Known allergy to fluoroquinolone (FQ) antibiotics or a history of severe tendinopathy related to FQs. Concurrent use of medications that prolong the cardiac QT interval. Documented prior treatment for MDR-TB. Recent treatment with antibiotics active against MDR-TB. Severe blistering reaction to tuberculin. End-stage liver failure (Child-Pugh Class C). Dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease. Abnormal baseline liver function tests (aspartate or alanine aminotransferase levels >3 times the upper limit of normal). End-stage kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <20 mL/min). Platelet count <50 × 10⁹ cells/L. Baseline electrocardiogram showing a QT segment >450 ms in adults. The study also included adult index patients who met the following criteria: Age ≥18 years. Bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB diagnosed from a sputum sample. Treatment for MDR-TB initiated within the preceding 6 months. Genotypic or phenotypic resistance to isoniazid (INH) and rifampin (RIF). The study was conducted in Vietnam, another high-incidence country for TB and MDR/RR-TB, across urban and rural settings in 10 provinces. Study sites adhered to the National Tuberculosis Programme (NTP) guidelines for managing drug-resistant TB. Participants were randomized into treatment groups, with households assigned to either levofloxacin (Lfx) or placebo. Randomization was computer-generated, and the study was double-blinded, meaning neither participants nor researchers knew the treatment allocation. Chest X-rays (CXR) were performed at baseline and during follow-up if TB symptoms or signs were present. IGRA and HIV testing were conducted at baseline, and pregnancy tests were performed for menstruating female participants. Blood tests, including full blood count, alanine transaminase, and bilirubin, were collected at baseline. Children were followed at regular intervals (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48, and 72 weeks) and during unscheduled visits as needed. At each visit, clinical assessments for TB symptoms, new TB exposure, and adverse events were conducted. Medication adherence was monitored through pill counts, treatment diaries, and questionnaires. Weight and height were measured, and concomitant medications and healthcare visits were documented. Medication doses were adjusted monthly as necessary. Respiratory samples were collected for mycobacterial evaluation if TB symptoms or abnormal CXR findings were present. Sampling methods included induced sputum or gastric aspiration for children under 5 years and expectorated sputum for older children. Samples were analyzed using smear microscopy, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, and mycobacterial culture. Drug susceptibility testing was performed on all isolates. The primary study endpoint was bacteriologically confirmed TB, defined as a positive identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by culture or molecular diagnostic methods in a close contact with clinical or radiological evidence of TB disease. Secondary endpoints included all forms of TB (bacteriologically confirmed or clinically probable), therapy completion, treatment discontinuation due to adverse events, grade 3 or 4 adverse events, and all-cause mortality. Statistical analyses included intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol populations. Cox regression was used to estimate the hazard ratio for time to TB endpoint, accounting for household clustering and adjusting for site and age group. Safety analyses included all participants who received at least one dose of the study drug. An interim safety analysis assessed the rate of grade 3 and 4 adverse events after 600 participants completed 6 months of therapy. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of levofloxacin in reducing incident TB compared to placebo, with a target sample size adjusted based on assumed efficacy and prior meta-analysis data. Outcomes were adjudicated by blinded expert panels using clinical, radiological, microbiological, and molecular data.
